column2: The belly is threefold: hollow, thin (kshama), and full (a part and whole). The sides have five actions; the shank action is fivefold; the foot action is of many kinds, remembered in dance and drama.
Laughter with sound, sinful laughter, soundless, and excessive laughter. The one called pathetic is a sentiment of three kinds:
arising from injury to dharma, and born of play of mind; grief arises from sorrow, the abiding feeling — which is held the earlier-born.
By limbs, costume and speech the furious sentiment too is threefold; its producer is anger, sweat, horripilation and trembling.
The heroic: hero of gift, hero of dharma, hero of battle — three. The cause of its production is said to be energy (utsaha).
Where in beginnings the heroic alone follows — the sentiment named terrible has fear as its producer;
disturbing and agitating: the odious is remembered twofold; the disturbing by leaps and the like; the agitating by blood and the like;
disgust begins it; its sattvic part arises. The properties that make the beauty of poetry are called ornaments (alankara).
They are the adorners of word, meaning and both — threefold. Those which here are able to adorn the word by derivation and the like
are called word-ornaments by those knowing poetics: chhaya, mudra, ukti, yukti, gumphana,
vakovakya, anuprasa, chitra and dushkara — nine ornaments of words are to be known, without mixing.
Of these, imitation of another's speech is Chhaya, and that too is fourfold: by imitation of the single utterance of popular, clever, childish speech;
proverbial speech, popular speech — those are common to all; that which follows popular speech the wise desire as Chhaya.
The clever are the refined; refinement is intelligence skilled in arts; the Chhekokti expressing that is desired by poets as Chhaya.
Speech of the untrained is observed by all as childish speech; therefore Arbhakokti Chhaya imitates only that speech.
Speech with scrambled letters and indecent, of a drunken man — such is Mattokti; that Chhaya too shines greatly.
By a special intention, showing the poet's power, bringing delight — that is Mudra; that same is Shayya, not in my view.
That is called Ukti in which even the meaning is reasonable and pleases the hearts of the good by the rule of worldly conduct.
Command and prohibition, rule and non-rule, option and exclusion — six are its utterances.
The arrangement imagined for joining two, speakable and speaker, that are as if unrelated mutually, is called Yukti by the wise.
Word, word-meaning, sentence and sentence-meaning, subject, context, and expansion — thus sixfold.
Gumphana is the practice of composition concerning the order of words and meanings; by imitation of words, by sequence of meaning, by meaning — threefold in order.
A sentence with utterance and reply is Vakovakya, twofold: by the difference of straight and crooked speech, the first is natural speech;
that has two forms: with earlier question and with question first; Vakrokti arises by bhangi and kaku, twofold by that.
By whatever mode, whatever similarity is felt — closeness of words with that form and the like, Anuprasa, conveys sentiment.
In an assembly, delightful for the curious, a binding of speech is called Chitra: question, riddle, hidden, dropped, given, and both —
Samasya — seven are its divisions, by the questioning of various meanings. Where an answer is given with similar arrangement of letters,
that is a question; by division of one-asked and two-asked answers: the one-asked is twofold: compound and separate.
A riddle (prahelika) where the word is concealed for both meanings; it is twofold: of meaning and of word; the meaning one by understanding of meaning,
the verbal one by understanding of words — they call the riddle sixfold. Where even with part of the sentence hidden the meaning is not real,
with expectation arranged by that part — that is Gupta, and it is also Gudha. Where another meaning appears by dropping a part of the sentence and the like,
with expectation set by that part — that is Chyuta, fourfold by dropping of vowel, consonant, dot (anusvara) and visarga.
Where, even with the part of the sentence given, a second meaning is understood — they call it Datta; its divisions by vowels and the rest as before.
Where, in place of a removed letter, another letter placed shows another meaning — that is called Chyutadatta.
One closely joined verse made of portions of various verses — that is Samasya, by mingling of the work of another and one's own.
Made with great difficulty, showing the poet's ability — Dushkara — a great festival for the cultured even in lack of sentiment.
By rule, by Vidarbha (arrangement), and by binding it is threefold. The poet's vow of beautiful construction is remembered as rule.
By place, by vowel, by consonant it is threefold. Option is described by reverse and forward order;
reverse and forward arise by word and by meaning. Artistic invention by arrangement of letters of many meters
of those well-known objects is called Bandha. Gomutrika, Ardhabhramana, Sarvatobhadra, lotus,
wheel, wheel-lotus, staff and drum — eight kinds. In each half and each foot letters equal at alternate places;
twofold Gomutrika: the first, others call it Ashvapada; the last Gomutrika; they call the cow and net-binding.
By halves and half-feet one should make the arrangement of these two; of the letters placed here in their order below and below,
of letters standing below and below, one should carry up to the fourth foot; from the fourth foot one should carry upward the half-foot in reverse.
That same is Sarvatobhadra, threefold lotus; the four-petalled; then Vighna; both in the four-petalled.
Then of the first foot, the cerebral three-foot letter arises at the end of all the feet;
the last of the former foot at the beginning of the latter foot in reverse; the last of the last foot and two letters at the beginning of the first foot;
in a four-petal; in an eight-petal three letters again; in a sixteen-petal if there is alternate, one letter;
one should weigh the pericarp upward, a row of letters in petal-shape; one should enter on the pericarp in the four-petalled lotus;
one should write one on the pericarp, two each in the directions and corners; one should make entry and exit in the directions on the eight-petalled lotus;
of the uneven letters all around, enjoying so many rows of petals; in the middle the placing of equal letters in the sixteen-petalled lotus.
The wheel is twofold: four-spoked and six-spoked, there the first; in the first half equal letters, the first and fifth of the foot;
odd and Ashvayuj, the fourth and eighth; of that in the spokes east and west, in order,
four half-feet in the nave; its first letter; one should lead up to the western spoke; in the rim the two feet in the rest;
the third at the end of the fourth foot; the first two letters alike; of the three feet the tenth, if alike;
in the first and last of it six letters if in the west; they are at two intervals, then Brihat is told in order.
In two facing spokes one should write a foot each in order; in the nave the tenth letter; in the rim one should lead the fourth foot;
the first and last, the tenth of the verse equal; the first and last of the even; in the beginning the letter equal, fourth and fifth of the first and second;
if the third arises by reversal of the second, one should make the foot of the petal; staff, wheel-lotus, of the work;
second and first in the east petal alike, and seventh, and another; in the north petal alike; with the two seconds in the halves;
the second and sixth alike, fourth and fifth too; at the beginning and end feet equal; the seventh of the latter half;
equal; the fourth and fifth one should apply in order; the fourth should be applied likewise, at the petal ends in the feet in order;
the last and first of the halves in the drum alike; a letter fallen in the half-foot by reverse and forward;
one should bind the last up to the fourth, as the first; from the fourth foot as the first from the ninth, from the sixteenth too;
making four letters in the middle of the case, in the middle of the letter, one should make it so that it has a drum shape.
The second has the wealth of Chakra and Shardulavikridita; Gomutrika with all meters; the other Bandhas with Anushtubh.
If the name is not among them in the poet's and the poem's — friends are pleased; no enemy suffers thus.
Arrow, bow, sky, sword, mace, spear, two- and four-, three-horned, thunderbolt, pestle, goad,
foot of chariot, of elephant, lotus pond, sword-daughter — these Bandhas, and others, are to be known by the wise themselves.
Where two possessors are likened to each other equally, that is Paraspara-upama (mutual simile); in the reverse of their fame it would be otherwise;
Viparita-upama: Niyama-upama by exclusion; elsewhere, by continuation, it would be Aniyama-upama;
apart from Samuchchaya-upama, by declaring abundance of other properties; though a single property is equal, a difference is intended;
what is stated as excess is Vyatireka-upama; where the simile is with many like things, it is Bahu-upama;
if properties are many in each comparison, that is Mala-upama; by change of the comparison, equivalence is Vikriya-upama;
where the poet likens by projecting something impossible in the three worlds onto the counter-subject, it is known as Adbhuta-upama.
